Where to record a deed in Baltimore County

Deeds for Baltimore County property go to the Land Records department of the Circuit Court for Baltimore County, inside the Clerk's Office at the County Courts Building, 401 Bosley Avenue, 2nd Floor, Towson, MD 21204. The mailing address is P.O. Box 6754, Towson, MD 21285-6754, and the office is open weekdays from 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.

Each Maryland county and Baltimore City runs its own land records department inside the circuit court clerk's office. Baltimore City records its own deeds, so a property inside the independent city is not recorded in Towson.

What the land records office can record

The office records any instrument that affects a legal interest in real property, including deeds, mortgages, liens, powers of attorney and certain leases. Clerks accept documents that meet the requirements and reject those that do not. They cannot help fill out forms or review a document before it is recorded.

That rule is the main reason sellers use a title company or attorney. A rejected deed costs days, and when a closing date is set, days matter. Talk to a lawyer before recording a new deed.

Numbers worth saving from the Clerk's Office:

  • Land Records Recording: 410-887-2651
  • Land Records Indexing: 410-887-3088
  • Main number: 410-887-2601; TTY users can dial Maryland Relay at 711
  • Foreclosure department: 410-887-2652

Taxes due before a deed is recorded

Baltimore County collects its own transfer tax and the state recordation tax before the Clerk's Office takes a deed. The county's Office of Budget and Finance handles both at a separate counter. Bring payment to the Transfer and Recordation Section at 400 Washington Avenue, Room 154, Towson, MD 21204, with checks payable to Baltimore County, Maryland.

RequirementAmount or rule
Baltimore County transfer tax1.5% of consideration
State recordation tax$2.50 per $500 (or fraction of $500) of consideration, or of the principal debt secured
Lien certificateRequired for any deed that changes or transfers ownership; a deed without one will not be processed
Maryland State Intake SheetRequired with every deed and property-related document
Counter hoursMonday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.

The first $22,000 of consideration for a grantee's principal residence is exempt from the Baltimore County transfer tax. Call the Transfer Tax Section at 410-887-2416 to ask whether your deal qualifies before you count on that credit.

The contract should say which party pays each tax. Have the title company show every charge on the settlement statement.

Why a deed needs a lien certificate

The lien certificate lets the county confirm that no taxes or charges are owed on the property account before ownership changes. It costs $55, and you can apply in person or by mail with a self-addressed, stamped envelope.

Order it as soon as a contract is signed. If tax is owed, it must in most cases be paid before the transfer, which pushes a closing date if you discover a balance the day before settlement. Taxpayer Services at 410-887-2416 answers account questions.

Call before you plan a same-day pickup, since the lien certificate service can be interrupted during county system updates.

Deeds that need state assessment approval

Agricultural-use deeds and partial-transfer deeds must first be approved by the Maryland Department of Assessments and Taxation. The Towson office is at 300 East Joppa Road, Room 602.

If you are splitting a lot, build the approval into your timeline. A partial-transfer deed sent to the Clerk's Office without it risks rejection.

  • Whole-parcel residential deed: intake sheet, lien certificate, tax payment.
  • Agricultural-use deed: the same items plus approval from the assessments department.
  • Partial-transfer deed: the same items plus approval from the assessments department.

Can you e-record a deed in Baltimore County?

Under Maryland Rule 1-322, documents cannot be filed directly by electronic transmission, though the Clerk's site links an E-Recording for Land Records page under E-Services. Some Maryland counties accept deeds and other documents through Simplifile, and electronic signatures require an Affidavit of Intent to Use Electronic Signature, form CC094.

Ask your title company whether it uses an electronic channel in Baltimore County or delivers the deed in person. Deed-related messages from the county tax office arrive from one email address under the subject line Official Tax Notice. Add that sender to your safe list so the message is not lost in spam.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Baltimore County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Recording fees, payment and copies

The Clerk's Office accepts cash, MasterCard, Visa and Discover, plus checks or money orders payable to Clerk of the Circuit Court. Personal out-of-state checks and debit cards are refused. Land records fees are set in a separate Circuit Court fee schedule, so get the current amounts from the Clerk's Office before you bring payment.

For research, the Maryland State Archives runs a free viewer for deeds at landrec.msa.maryland.gov, and an account is required. Copies from the viewer cost $0.50 per page. Land records documents can also be requested from the Clerk's Office online or by email.

Fees on a Maryland deed are split. Some go to the land records department and some to the local county finance office, which is why you make one payment at the Clerk's Office and another at the county's Transfer and Recordation Section.

Recording steps for a seller

Closing day goes smoothly when the paperwork is ready in the right order. Your title company or attorney will normally handle these steps, and knowing them helps you ask the right questions.

  • Order the lien certificate and pay any balance it reveals.
  • Complete the Maryland State Intake Sheet for the deed.
  • Pay the county transfer tax and state recordation tax at the Transfer and Recordation Section.
  • Deliver the deed and the receipts to the Land Records counter and pay the recording fee there.
  • Request a copy of the recorded deed for your files.

An as-is cash sale uses the same recording steps. What it skips is the buyer's lender, so there is no appraisal or repair list standing between you and the closing table.

Inherited Baltimore County houses

An heir selling a Baltimore County house deals with more than the land records counter. The Clerk's Office lists a Register of Wills at 410-887-6680 and the Orphans' Court at 410-887-6516. Neither can stand in for a lawyer's advice.

If taxes were left unpaid, settle them with the Office of Budget and Finance at 410-887-2404 first, because the lien certificate will show them. The county steps above apply however the house is sold, including an as-is sale.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

Where is the Baltimore County Circuit Court land records office?

It is in the Clerk's Office at 401 Bosley Avenue, 2nd Floor, Towson, MD 21204, open weekdays from 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Land Records Recording is at 410-887-2651.

What is the Baltimore County transfer tax?

The county charges 1.5 percent of consideration. The first $22,000 of consideration for a grantee's principal residence is exempt.

What is the Maryland recordation tax on a Baltimore County deed?

The state recordation tax is $2.50 per $500, or fraction of $500, of consideration or of the debt secured. Checks go to Baltimore County, Maryland.

Do I need a lien certificate to record a deed in Baltimore County?

Yes. Any deed that changes or transfers ownership needs one, and a deed without it will not be processed. The fee is $55.

Does the Clerk's Office help me fill out a deed?

No. Clerks cannot help fill out forms or review documents before recording, so speak with a lawyer or your title company first.

Which office records a deed in Montgomery County?

The Land Records department of the Montgomery County Circuit Court records deeds, mortgages and releases for the whole county. Rockville is the county seat, and the court's land records staff are split into desks for recording, indexing, copies and public questions. The county's land records page lists each one:

DeskPhoneUse it for
Recording Department240-777-9470Submitting documents
Public Information Room240-777-9477Questions about land documents
Indexing Department240-777-9476Grantor and grantee name indexes
Duplication Department240-777-9480Copies and certified copies

The Public Information Room is in the North Tower, second floor, Room 2120, and is open 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. on weekdays. Recording closes earlier, at 4:00 p.m. A seller who is bringing a deed in person on the day of settlement should plan around that cutoff.

How can I look up a Montgomery County deed or lien for free?

MDLandRec, run by the Maryland State Archives at landrec.msa.maryland.gov, is free to search. First-time users apply for a login with a valid email address, and the password usually arrives within about an hour on a business day.

The system lets you search by name, by liber and folio, or by tax account number, and you can print what you find. It covers land records, plats, liens, judgments and financing statements. For a seller, that is the quickest way to see whether an old mortgage, a judgment lien or an unreleased deed of trust is still attached to the title.

Two limits are worth knowing. Plats are on a separate site, PLATS.NET, and the county says it does not keep individual house location plats. Equity index books from 1777 to 1981 are held by the Maryland State Archives rather than the courthouse.

What does it cost to record a deed in Montgomery County?

The statewide circuit court fee schedule effective September 2, 2026 sets the recording fee for an instrument involving solely a principal residence at $60. The county page adds a $40 surcharge on recordable instruments, continued by Chapter 538 of the 2020 legislative session.

ItemFee
Instrument involving solely a principal residence$60
Other instrument, 9 pages or less$60
Other instrument, 10 pages or more$115
Release, 9 pages or less$50
Copy, per page$0.50
Certified copy$5 plus $0.50 per page
Surcharge on recordable instruments$40

The schedule comes from the Maryland Judiciary. Fee schedules change, so call the Recording Department to confirm the total for your document before settlement.

How much recordation tax does Montgomery County charge?

Montgomery County's recordation tax is built from three layers, and it climbs once the price passes $500,000. The County Council's economic impact statement for Bill 17-23 describes the structure in force before the 2023 change: a base rate of $2.08 per $500, a school increment of $2.37 per $500, and a premium of $2.30 per $500 on the portion above $500,000.

The council enacted Bill 17-23 on May 9, 2023, on a 7 to 4 vote, and the new rates took effect October 1, 2023. The base and school rates stayed put. Only the premium changed, and it now rises with the price:

Recordation amountPremium rate
$600,000 to $750,000$5.75 per $500
Over $750,000 to $1 million$6.33 per $500
Over $1 million$6.90 per $500

For scale, the same impact statement lists the old-law tax on a $500,000 sale at $4,450. The county's release states that the one percent county transfer tax was unchanged, while the state legislative table says Montgomery sets variable transfer tax rates by property value. Confirm the exact figure for your price with the county Department of Finance, which is at 101 Monroe Street, 15th Floor, Rockville.

Are there recordation tax breaks for buyers in Montgomery County?

Yes. The impact statement notes that first-time homebuyers get the first $100,000 of the sale price exempted from the base recordation rate. It also says the first $100,000 of value goes untaxed for a home occupied at least seven months in its first year. The same statement says that $100,000 exemption does not cover refinancing, second homes or commercial deals.

The statutory basis is Maryland's recordation law, which lets each county exempt a set amount for owner-occupied homes. For a seller, these breaks matter because they affect how much a buyer pays at settlement and how the parties divide the closing taxes under the Maryland default rule.

What does a house sale in Montgomery County look like on the numbers?

Montgomery County is the most populous county in Maryland, with 1,062,061 residents in the 2020 census, and the Census Bureau's 2020 to 2024 survey shows a market that skews toward owners. The figures below come from the Census QuickFacts table.

MeasureMontgomery County
Housing units (July 1, 2025)419,402
Households (2020 to 2024)389,210
Owner-occupied rate65.3%
Median gross rent$2,068
Median monthly owner costs with a mortgage$2,929
Lived in the same house a year earlier88.1%

Land area is 493.11 square miles, which works out to 2,153.8 people per square mile in 2020. The county was created in 1776 from part of Frederick County. Its rolling Piedmont terrain runs from near sea level along the Potomac to about 875 feet north of Damascus.

Where are the main communities and employers around Montgomery County land records?

Sellers in the county are spread across incorporated cities and large unincorporated places, and every deed goes to the same Rockville land records office. Rockville, Gaithersburg and Takoma Park are incorporated. Bethesda, Silver Spring, Germantown, Aspen Hill and Wheaton are census-designated places, and Germantown is the most populous unincorporated area.

The employer base is heavy on government and health care. Wikipedia's 2021 list names the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Montgomery County Public Schools, the county government, the Department of Defense and Adventist Healthcare among the largest. The county is also home to the NIH and FDA, and it is a major biotechnology hub with a GDP above $117 billion in 2024.

Montgomery County Public Schools is the largest district in Maryland, with about 162,000 students. Transit includes both arms of the Metro Red Line, MARC commuter rail, Ride On buses and the Flash bus rapid transit line, and the Purple Line is scheduled to open in 2027.

What should a Montgomery County seller bring to the recording step?

The title company or settlement attorney normally handles recording, but a seller should still know what has to be in the packet. The county page and the state fee schedule point to these items.

  • The signed deed, with the exemption claim written out if the transfer is exempt from tax
  • The recordation and transfer tax amounts due on the deed
  • Releases for any mortgage being paid off, recorded at the $50 release fee for documents of 9 pages or less

Montgomery County also posts a notice about transfer-on-death deeds and notices of death filings on its land records page. An heir selling a parent's house should check whether one was recorded.

Frequently asked questions

Where do I record a deed in Montgomery County, Maryland?

Deeds are recorded by the Land Records department of the Montgomery County Circuit Court in Rockville. The Recording Department can be reached at 240-777-9470, and recording hours end at 4:00 p.m.

How much does it cost to record a Montgomery County deed?

The statewide fee schedule effective September 2, 2026 lists $60 for an instrument involving solely a principal residence, plus the $40 surcharge on recordable instruments, before recordation and transfer taxes. Call the Recording Department to confirm the total for your document.

Did Montgomery County raise its recordation tax?

Yes. Bill 17-23, enacted May 9, 2023, raised the premium rate for amounts above $600,000 starting October 1, 2023, while the base and school rates stayed the same.

Can I search Montgomery County land records online?

Yes. MDLandRec at landrec.msa.maryland.gov is free after you register with an email address, and you can search by name, liber and folio, or tax account number.

Who pays the recordation and transfer tax on a sale?

Maryland presumes the buyer and seller split them equally unless the contract or law says otherwise. For a first-time buyer who will occupy the home, the seller pays them unless the parties expressly agree otherwise.

Where do I record a deed in Prince George's County?

Recording takes two stops in person: the county Office of Finance in Largo, then the Land Records Division of the Circuit Court in Upper Marlboro. The court's deed processing page lays out the order, and the county step comes first.

StepOfficeAddress and hours
1Office of Finance1301 McCormick Drive, Suite 1100, Largo; 301-952-4030; 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. weekdays
2Land Records Division14701 Governor Oden Bowie Drive, Room J1108, Upper Marlboro; 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. weekdays

Bring the original deed, one full copy, and the State of Maryland land instrument intake sheet. A deed that claims an exemption from recording fees or state transfer tax has to cite every applicable code section from the Maryland Annotated Code. The Land Records Division itself answers at 301-780-2253, and the courthouse main line is 301-952-3655.

What does it cost to record a deed in Prince George's County?

The county's fee page lists $20 for an instrument of 1 to 9 pages, and that fee covers every page when the instrument concerns a principal residence. A $40 surcharge sits on top for recorded documents. The statewide circuit court schedule that takes effect September 2, 2026 lists $60 for a principal residence instrument, so the two sources disagree and the amount should be confirmed by phone.

ServiceCounty fee page
Other instrument, 1 to 9 pages (all pages if principal residence)$20
Other instrument, 10 or more pages, not a principal residence$75
Release, 1 to 9 pages$10
Surcharge on recorded documents (not powers of attorney, plats, chattel)$40
Copy of a deed or other document$2
Copy of a deed of trust or mortgage$5
Certified copy of a deed of trust or mortgage$10
Certified copy, other instruments$7

Payment is due when the document is recorded. The office takes cash, checks, money orders and credit cards, with checks and money orders payable to The Clerk of the Circuit Court. Documents come back by mail when you supply a return address, and otherwise they wait for pickup.

What transfer and recordation taxes apply in Prince George's County?

The county transfer tax is 1.4%, set under County Code sections 10-187 and 10-188, and the state recordation tax is $5.50 per $1,000 of consideration. The county's Finance Affidavit instructions put the recordation figure as $2.75 per $500, rounded up to the next $500, and the state legislative rate table lists the same $2.75. The state transfer tax of 0.5% comes on top.

TaxRateAuthority
County transfer tax1.4%County Code 10-187 and 10-188
Recordation tax$5.50 per $1,000Maryland Tax-Property Article, collected by the county
State transfer tax0.5%, or 0.25% for a qualifying first-time buyerTax-Property 13-203

The court's Land Records page sends questions about the state transfer tax to the Land Records Division and questions about county transfer and recordation tax to the Office of Finance. On a $400,000 sale, 1.4% county transfer tax alone comes to $5,600, so the split between buyer and seller is worth settling in the contract. Maryland's default is an equal split unless the contract or a law says otherwise.

What is the Finance Affidavit, and who needs it?

The Finance Affidavit is the form Prince George's County uses to claim an exemption from the county transfer tax or the state recordation tax. The county says every instrument recorded in its land records is taxable unless Maryland's code or the county code exempts it, and the affidavit is how a filer names the exemption.

Most of its clauses concern loans and refinances:

  • Clause A: a principal residence refinance, where recordation tax applies to the difference between the new loan and the unpaid principal balance.
  • Clause B-1: a principal residence with a purchase money deed of trust recorded for more than 12 months, covering new loans, modifications and home equity lines.
  • Clause B-2: a refinance by a borrower who does not qualify for B-1, paired with Clause A.
  • Clause C: a refinance of a non-principal residence or investment property, where the 1.4% county transfer tax applies to the difference between the new and original loan amounts.

The property must be the borrower's principal residence in state assessment records. The county's instructions list the Treasury as the contact for submission details.

What disclosures does Maryland require for Prince George's County sales?

Prince George's County has its own line items in the state's residential contract statute. Section 14-117 of the Real Property Article requires, where deferred private water and sewer assessments are recorded, that the contract disclose eight items, including the assessment amount, remaining payments, interest rate, payoff amount, and that prepayment carries no penalty. Those assessments cannot be amortized over more than 20 years.

The contract also has to disclose whether a development impact fee was imposed on the property, the total amount, and any unpaid balance. Statewide, every residential sale needs a homestead property tax credit statement, and one- or two-unit contracts need the statement that recordation and transfer taxes are shared equally unless negotiated otherwise.

What kind of place is Prince George's County?

Prince George's County borders Washington, D.C. on its west side, and it was created on April 23, 1696 from parts of Charles and Calvert counties. It covers 499 square miles, 483 of them land, and the 2020 census counted 967,201 residents, which makes it the second-most populous county in Maryland. Upper Marlboro is the county seat, though some government functions have moved to the Largo area since 1991.

U.S. Route 50 roughly divides North and South County. Informal regions include North County, Central County, the Rural Tier, the Inner Beltway and South County. Bowie is the largest city, at 58,329 people in 2020, and other cities and towns include Laurel, College Park, Greenbelt and Hyattsville. Large unincorporated communities include Largo, Clinton, Oxon Hill, Fort Washington and National Harbor.

The county has the only Potomac River waterfront in Maryland, and the Patuxent River forms its eastern border. The western edge near Montgomery County rises into the Piedmont above 300 feet, while most of the county is Atlantic Coastal Plain with gently rolling hills.

Who are the big employers and how do people get around?

Federal and university jobs lead the 2021 employer list on Wikipedia:

  • Joint Base Andrews, 18,000 jobs
  • University System of Maryland, 13,000
  • NASA Goddard Space Flight Center, 12,200
  • University of Maryland Capital Region Health, 4,800
  • IRS, 4,500, and the U.S. Census Bureau, 4,285
  • UPS, 3,300, and MGM National Harbor, 2,400

The Washington Metro has 15 stations in the county, including terminals at Greenbelt, New Carrollton, Largo and Branch Avenue. MARC's Camden and Penn lines also serve it, TheBus runs county routes, and a water taxi leaves from National Harbor. The Purple Line is slated to open in 2027. Reagan National, BWI and Dulles are the nearby airports. The school system is Prince George's County Public Schools.

What property tax facts matter to a Prince George's County seller?

The county real property rate is $1.0000 per $100 of assessed value for fiscal 2026, the county Treasury says, with the state adding $0.1120 and Park and Planning adding $0.2940. The county's Tax Facts sheet says unpaid taxes can lead to a lien sold at the annual tax sale on the second Monday in May.

The county caps the taxable assessment increase for fiscal 2026 at 3%, while the state cap is 10% after the first full tax year. In the state's 2024 tax sale survey, Prince George's County advertised 4,283 properties, offered 2,206, and sold 2,003 liens, while 1,146 properties were redeemed before foreclosure in fiscal 2024. The county's Homeowner Protection Program may keep a limited-income home out of tax sale for at least three years, though enrollment is limited.

Frequently asked questions

Where is the Prince George's County land records office?

The Land Records Division is in the Judiciary Administrative Services Building at 14701 Governor Oden Bowie Drive, Room J1108, in Upper Marlboro. It is open 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. on weekdays.

Do I pay the county first or the court first?

The county Office of Finance in Largo comes first, then the Land Records Division in Upper Marlboro. Call 301-952-4030 for the Finance step.

What is the Prince George's County transfer tax rate?

It is 1.4% under County Code 10-187 and 10-188. The state also charges a 0.5% transfer tax and a recordation tax of $5.50 per $1,000.

Can I search Prince George's County land records online?

Yes. The court points to the Land Records Online Search at landrec.msa.maryland.gov, which shows recorded and verified land records volumes. Clerks cannot give legal advice or run title searches.

Why do two sources show different recording fees?

The county fee page lists $20 for a principal residence instrument, while the statewide schedule effective September 2, 2026 lists $60. Call 301-780-2253 to confirm the current amount before you record.
